en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Matrix of the Mirror of Poetics.
The ministers and chaplains of kings who rule according to the Dhamma,
having thoroughly relied upon the science of polity (nītisattha), determine legal judgments.
The constituent parts are the four Vedas, along with the detailed expositions of Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya.
The Dhammasattha and the Purāṇa— these are the fourteen branches of knowledge (vijjā).
The Āyubbeda, Manubbeda, and Gandhabba— these three,
together with the Atthasattha as the fourth, are considered the eighteen branches of knowledge.
The Sutisamutisaṅkhyā, the Rogānīti as a distinction,
the Gandhabbā, the Gaṇikā, the Dhanubbedā, and the Pūraṇā;
the Tikicchā, the Itihāsa, the Jotimāyā, and the Chanda.
The Ketumantas, the Saddas, and these eighteen branches of craft—these are known as "Dama" (the taming).
The wielder of the rod is called the lord of the earth;
his method is "Daṇḍanīti" (the science of government), which is also termed "Nayanānīti" (the science of guidance).
Because this world is led by punishment, or because it leads punishment,
it is known as *Daṇḍanīti* (the Science of Punishment), which prevails throughout the three worlds.
I shall here declare the Compendium of Royal Policy (*Rājanīti-samuccaya*), extracted from various treatises.
This is the "Sword" that destroys all seeds, the *Cāṇakya-sārasaṅgaha*.
I shall proclaim the root text (*mūlasutta*) as it was spoken by Cāṇakya;
by the mere knowledge of which, even a fool becomes wise.
Gaining of friends, the breaking of friendships, conflict, and reconciliation; likewise,
the five types of indolence and other matters— these topics are written by Kassapa from the *Lokanīti*.

(1) The Section on the Wise Man (*Paṇḍitakaṇḍa*). (2) The Section on the Good Person (*Sujanakaṇḍa*). (3) The Section on the Foolish and the Wicked (*Bāladujjanakaṇḍa*). (4) The Section on Friends (*Mittakaṇḍa*). (5) The Section on Women (*Itthikaṇḍa*). (6) The Section on Kings (*Rājakaṇḍa*). (7) The Miscellaneous Section (*Pakiṇṇakakaṇḍa*). — *Lokanīti*:
The sections on the wise man and the good person, the wicked, friends, and women.
And the *Rājapakiṇṇaka*: thus adorned are the seven chapters.
This was edited by Cakkindābhisiri at Kāsika and Sāka;
on the sixth day of the second half of the month of Channa, in the seventh year of the Kāla era.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem in brief according to the Magadha tradition, I shall proclaim the *Lokanīti*, extracted from various treatises.
In this world, ethical conduct (*nīti*) is the essence of a man.
Mother, father, teacher, and friend—
therefore, a person should understand this principle;
thus one becomes wise, great, and possessed of much learning.
The Great Priceless Ethics:
(1) Discourse on the Wise Man; (2) Discourse on Dissension; (3) Discourse on Friends; (4) Discourse on the Leader; (5) Discourse on Women.
For the Sage Rahasakya, the hindrance is craving.
I pay homage to the most excellent Bodhi tree, beautiful to behold and ever-freed.
Herein, the essence of conduct for living beings consists of friends, teachers, and parents;
one who possesses such conduct is wise, intelligent, competent, learned, and endowed with insight into the true goal.
The Discourse on the Principles of Dhamma: (1) Discourse on Teachers, (2) Discourse on Crafts, (3) Discourse on Wisdom, (4) Discourse on Learning, (5) Discourse on Narratives,
(6) Discourse on Wealth, (7) Discourse on Countries, (8) Discourse on Dependence, (9) Discourse on Friends, (10) Discourse on Evil People, (11) Discourse on Good People.
(12) Discourse on strength; (13) discourse on women; (14) discourse on chariots; (15) discourse on slaves; (16) discourse on household life; (17) discourse on what ought to be done;
(18) discourse on what ought not to be done; (19) discourse on what ought to be known; (20) discourse on ornaments; (21) discourse on the duties of kings;
(22) discourse on attendants; (23) discourse on a mixture of suffering and so forth; (24) miscellaneous discourse.
Victor over those who possess wheels and those beyond them, Lord of gods and supreme among gods,
Brahmā and Lord of Brahmās— may the Conqueror fulfill my aspiration.
May he long remain in the world, the destroyer of all beings' suffering.
Having paid homage to the most excellent Jewel, which triumphs over the darkness of great delusion and shines forth as the Teaching of the Conqueror, and relying upon my venerable predecessors,
I shall proclaim the Dhamma of ethics, which brings happiness to the entire world.
The teacher and the craft, the wealth of wisdom, learning, and speech;
the country, the support, the friend, the wicked person, and the strength of the virtuous;
the wife, the son, the slave, the household life, and what has been done or left undone.
The Ornament to be known, the One who practices the Duties of a King,
that which is mixed with suffering and so forth, and Miscellaneous— this is the summary outline (mātikā). Regarding the "Conduct of Kings" (rājanīti):
The lion [performed] one, the crane one, the cock trained four;
the crow five, the king named [the horse] six, Sunakkhatta three, and the donkey three.
Whether it be a great deed or a small one, whatever deed he wishes to perform—
One should act with all one's effort; at that time, one should be like a lion in one respect.
One should be well-restrained in the sense faculties, becoming wise like a crane;
by shedding the feathers of one’s hair [through austerity], one should accomplish all tasks.
Former standing, battle, sharing, and kinship;
the woman’s misconduct, and what was eaten—these four a cock should learn.
Secret sexual intercourse, looking [at others], food, and gathering kinsmen.
Having observed the watchfulness of the crow, one should train in five things:
vigilance, constant hope, cleanliness, readiness to wake, firm devotion, and courage.
These six qualities are found in those who have trained in them.
Wearied, it carries its burden, heeding neither cold nor heat;
it is always contented—one should train in these three qualities like a donkey.
A wise person here should practice these twenty virtues.
He shall conquer all enemies and become possessed of splendor.

(1) The Section on the Wise (Paṇḍitakaṇḍa), (2) the Section on the Virtuous (Sujanakaṇḍa), (3) the Section on the Foolish and Wicked (Bāladujjanakaṇḍa), (4) the Section on Friends (Mittakaṇḍa), (5) the Section on Kings (Rājakaṇḍa),

(6) the Section on Leaders (Nāyakakaṇḍa), (7) the Section on Sons (Puttakaṇḍa), (8) the Section on Physicians and Teachers (Vejjācariyakaṇḍa), (9) the Section on Slaves (Dāsakakaṇḍa), (10) the Section on Women (Itthikaṇḍa), (11) the Miscellaneous Section (Pakiṇṇakakaṇḍa).
If one brings the mirror of poetry (*kavidappaṇanīti*) to the forefront of speech,
then that person is indeed wise and of a scholarly nature in the midst of the world.
*The Mirror of Poetry* (*Kavidappaṇanīti*)
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
I pay homage to the Triple Gem:
to the Buddha, the Great Poet, and to the Dhamma practiced by him.
I bow my head in reverence to the stainless Sangha.
I shall, in brief, set forth for the benefit of poets this treatise on ethics titled *Kavidappana*, extracted from various scriptures.
The Essence of Ethics (Nītisāra) by Paṇḍitakaṇḍa is for humanity a friend and a teacher,
as well as a mother, a father, one possessed of ethics, learned, and a composer of books.
Whence can one who is lazy acquire a craft? Whence can one without a craft acquire wealth?
Whence can one without wealth have friends? Whence can one without friends have happiness?
Whence can one without happiness perform merit? Whence can one without merit attain excellence?
One who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words,
and performs well-done deeds is a wise person who follows the path of the virtuous.
Like a goldsmith who has fashioned a sword-blade from refined gold, he is polished by his own wisdom.
They produce delightful ornaments such as the *gajjapajja* and others. Greatness,
swiftness of grasp, correct retention, and non-forgetfulness of what has been grasped—
this is the characteristic of one who is easy to instruct.
One who is wise should contemplate knowledge and its goal as if they were free from aging and death;
one should practice the Dhamma as if seized by the hair by Death himself.
There is no wealth equal to a craft; thieves do not carry off a craft.
In this world, skill is a friend, and it brings happiness in the world beyond.
One should not say that the mouth exists merely for eating or for speaking;
rather, the wise person is one whose speech is like the wind—blown forth from the mouth.
Praise from fools and censure from the wise— of these two,
censure by the wise is better than praise from the foolish. Regarding that which is inconceivable,
accompanied by the commentary, spoken by the Conqueror, the wise person...
One who serves their teacher properly should always receive instruction.
Therefore, the wise person should always receive instruction from the profound words of the Victor,
together with their commentaries, while serving their teacher properly.
For one who lacks the instruction of a teacher does not find the essence of the meaning;
deprived of the essence of the meaning, he falls away from the True Dhamma.
But one who receives the instruction of a teacher and is endowed with the essence of the meaning—
One who protects the true Dhamma does not fall away from the true Dhamma.
Among all things, wisdom alone is said to be the supreme thing,
because it is never exhausted, because it is priceless, and because it is imperishable at all times.
Even with a small load, the wise and discerning person uplifts themselves,
like a tiny fire that blazes up when fanned.
All virtues reside in the wise, while faults belong solely to the deluded.
Therefore, among thousands of deluded ones, a single wise person stands out as superior.
Fools of poor intellect are envious, yet the virtuous man acts without fault;
the wise man is heavy with dignity, while the ignorant man is equal to them in his lack of discernment.
One should speak only what is pleasing, never what is displeasing;
for one who speaks what is pleasing, a heavy burden was lifted,
and he obtained wealth, whereby he became glad at heart.
Knowledge bestows discipline, and through discipline one attains maturity;
from maturity one acquires wealth, from wealth comes Dhamma, and from that, happiness.
Those people skilled in the Dhamma who honor their elders—
Praised in this very life and attaining a happy destination in the world beyond—
He who looks upon the wives of others as his own mother,
upon the wealth of others as a clod of earth, and upon all beings as himself— he is wise.
A wise person should indeed aspire, and not become despondent,
regarding blameless deeds praised by the virtuous.
A wise person should indeed aspire, and not become despondent.
I see myself as I have become, just as I had wished.
A wise person should indeed strive and not grow weary in the bases for meritorious action that are praised by the wise.
What is there that people who possess perseverance cannot achieve in this world?
Even across the ocean, they build a great bridge with hosts of monkeys.
What is the use of a noble lineage for a man who is devoid of virtue?
Even one who is unlearned, if he knows the scriptures, is honored even by the deities.
They desire a hero in times of crisis, one free from curiosity among counselors,
one who is dear in matters of food and drink, and a wise man when a matter of importance has arisen.
Those endowed with beauty and youth, born of a noble lineage,
do not shine if they are devoid of knowledge, like white cranes without their plumage.
One who has lived the holy life with clear wisdom knows the goal and crosses over.
In the mirror of the radiance of poetry (*sūrappabhā*), one sees a reflection, but not in the ocean of prose (*mākara*).
Yet the blind man lacks grammar; the deaf man is bereft of the treasury of words;
the cripple is devoid of literary composition; and the mute is deprived of logic.
The wise man, knowing various things and perceiving the vulnerabilities of others,
having brought all his enemies under his control, may be happy like a weaver. Even this great fire,
though possessing such power, cannot soften clay.
Water makes water soft, and kind speech makes the harsh soft.
A son who is neither wise nor righteous is merely a burden;
what is the use of a blind eye? It causes nothing but pain.
One conquers an enemy through gentleness; one conquers the cruel through gentleness.
There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by gentleness; therefore, one should conquer through gentleness.
By the birth of such a person, the lineage attains great elevation.
In the cycle of wandering through rebirths, who is there that dies and is not born again?
But for one who does not crave fame for generosity, austerity, or heroism,
nor seeks the attainment of supernormal knowledge, there is only the supreme mastery.
A single virtuous son is better than a hundred fools;
a single moon dispels the darkness, whereas the host of stars cannot do so.
By whom asceticism—which is exceedingly difficult to practice anywhere—is performed, that person is one who has reached the ford of merit.
His son should be a year old, accomplished, righteous, and pure.
He should be fondled for five years, spanked for ten years;
when he reaches his sixteenth year, one should treat him like a friend.
In pampering there are many faults, while in striking there are many virtues;
therefore, one should strike both a son and a pupil, but never pamper them.
The Magadha language, the vernacular, and the terminology of the Sakkatas [are used].
Among these, the wise and discerning person, being steadfast, should purify the textual tradition (*pāḷi*).
Six languages are proclaimed: Pāli, Prakrit, Apabhraṃśa, Paiśācī, Māgadhī, and Saurasenī.
Sandalwood is cool in the world, and moonlight is cooler than that;
yet well-spoken words are better even than sandalwood and moonlight.
A few well-spoken words uttered at the right time are truly excellent.
Even poor food, when eaten by one who is joyful, may have a sweet taste.
Though there be many teachers with much talk, they are not respected if they speak excessively;
has it not been seen that river water is beneficial even when it flows indifferently?
The stone parasol is heavy; beyond that, the instruction of the gods;
beyond that, the exhortation of the elders; beyond that, the teaching of the Buddha.
Cotton is light in the world; beyond that, one who is by nature fickle.
Therefore, his disciple thereafter becomes a wanderer who is negligent regarding the Dhamma.
Punishment for the wise is inflicted by the fool;
but the wise man, when praised by another wise man, is truly well-praised.
Among hundreds one is born a hero; among thousands, a scholar;
among hundreds of thousands, a donor may or may not appear.
Wisdom and kingship are never equal at any time.
A king is honored by the virtuous, and the wise are honored everywhere.
The virtuous are long-lived and the cause of happiness for all beings;
but the wicked are undoubtedly the cause of suffering for everyone.
When there is one wise and virtuous person, all people become virtuous;
when there is one tree with the fragrance of heartwood, all trees seem to be made of fragrance.
If even oneself is disciplined, the great masses will be led forth.
All go forth disciplined; what wise person would destroy that?
There is a vast and ultimate difference between the body and its virtues:
the body perishes in an instant, while the virtues endure for an eon.
Rivers drink no water; a tree eats no fruit;
the cloud cares not for the crop; the wealth of the virtuous is for the sake of others.
"Truth! Truth again!"—so crying out with uplifted arms, one is liberated.
There is no benefit for oneself at all, nor indeed any benefit for others, for one who does not act with restraint.
The mind of the virtuous does not undergo transformation through harsh words;
it is impossible to heat the waters of the ocean with grass torches.
Just as a solid block of stone is not moved by the wind,
so the wise do not waver amidst blame and praise. For one who possesses not even one of these—
virtue, wealth, desire, or liberation— [there is no benefit].
For one who merely grinds their own neck, birth is indeed useless.
Without even considering the work to be done, one should not abandon one's own effort;
for by merely grinding, oil cannot be obtained from sesame seeds.
For just as a chariot cannot move with only one wheel,
so too, without human effort, no action is accomplished.
Indeed, it is through exertion that tasks are fulfilled, not by mere wishful thinking.
For deer do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion.
A child comes to possess the qualities practiced by his mother and father;
one does not become wise merely by being born from a womb.
One whose mother is an enemy and whose father is a foe, by whom the child has not been educated,
does not shine in the midst of an assembly, like a crane in the midst of swans.
Even glass, through contact with gold, assumes the luster of an emerald.
Likewise, one who is surrounded by the virtuous, though deluded,
attains proficiency. Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should properly acquire skill in the syllables,
while correctly attending upon a teacher with the five qualities beginning with exertion.
Through diligence, attentiveness, a desire to hear, and service;
by learning a craft with respect, the wise person pleases their teacher.
For the intelligent, time passes in the diversion of literary arts.
For those deluded by misfortune, or by the root of strife and quarrel—
these six faults must be abandoned here by a man desiring prosperity:
sleep, sloth, fear, anger, laziness, and procrastination.
The person who is habitually sleepy, habitually socializing, who does not rise for his duties,
who is lazy and characterized by anger— this is the gateway to ruin.
Even toward beings devoid of virtue, the righteous show compassion.
For the moon does not withdraw its radiance even when in the house of an outcaste.
Where there is no person of wisdom, even one of slight virtue is honored;
in a place where the foot of purpose is absent, even the castor-oil plant is treated as a tree.
The teeth, hair, and nails of men do not shine when displaced from their proper positions.
Having understood this, the wise person should not abandon their own place.
Indeed, it is easy for everyone to display wisdom regarding the instructions of others.
The wise praise heedfulness in the performance of meritorious deeds for anyone, however great they may be, who personally undertakes the practice of the Dhamma.
Being heedful, the wise person attains both goals.
One should associate with such a wise person, one who points out faults, who speaks with restraint, and who is discerning—
just as one would seek the opener of a treasure.
For one who associates with such a person, it becomes better, not worse.
If a wise person attends upon one who is learned even for a moment, they quickly understand the Dhamma, just as the tongue perceives the flavor of soup.
Rare is the thoroughbred man; he is not born everywhere.
Wherever that wise one is born, that family prospers in happiness.
Just as a man who wraps tagara with leaves causes even the petals to waft a sweet fragrance, so it is through attending upon the wise.
One who seeks the meaning of what has been heard should listen attentively to the skilled, having investigated [the matter].
Just as food cooked in a pan may likewise be placed in a vessel, one should not despise even a small amount [of learning];
one should deposit what has been heard within the mind.
Like a drop of water on an ant-hill, it fills up only after a long time.
A centipede travels even hundreds of leagues as it goes,
yet the female crane, though coming from afar, does not go even a single step.
Not in every stream is there a jewel; not in every mountain is there a pearl;
not in every forest is there sandalwood; and not in every place is there a wise man.
Wherever a wise man endowed with learning is found—if such a learned one exists—there he may be sought.
One who seeks learning must go to that place with great effort,
even at the risk of one's life. That craft which is found only in books,
and that wealth which is in another's hand, is neither craft nor wealth when the time for need actually arises.
One may know the depth of water by the blue lotus, a person’s lineage by their conduct,
the measure of one's eloquence by their speech, and the richness of the soil by the grass.
One may know the extent of the water by the garland of white water-lilies.
The measure of a family is the measure of discipline;
the measure of eloquence is speech already spoken;
the measure of the earth is a withered blade of grass.
A person of little learning, though his knowledge is meager, considers himself wise, like a frog who has never seen the waters of the Indus and thinks only of the water in a well.
In the first stage of life one should acquire a craft; in the second, one should seek wealth.
One should practice the Dhamma in the third [life]; this is the natural law for people.
Desire to hear increases what has been heard; what has been heard increases wisdom.
Through wisdom one understands the meaning; the meaning understood brings happiness.
There is no friend equal to knowledge, nor any enemy equal to disease;
there is no love equal to wealth, nor any power equal to karma.
A hero should not go onto the battlefield without his weapon.
Whether he be a scholar, a traveler, or a merchant journeying to a foreign land,
a wise person should not disclose his loss of wealth, mental anguish, misconduct at home, deception, or humiliation.
Leading others astray, speaking much without being asked,
and proclaiming one's own virtues— these are the three types of inferior persons.
A swan does not shine among crows, nor does a lion shine among sheep.
A horse among camels, like a wise man among fools—
he who knows speech suited to the occasion, words pleasant according to one's nature,
and anger appropriate to oneself, he is a wise man.
A formless thing may have great luster, one of little wisdom may be a teacher,
a jar with little water may be shaken, and a cow with little milk may be restless.
A king has no satiety for wealth, nor does even a wise man for well-spoken words.
One never tires of gazing upon a lovely eye, nor does the ocean ever tire of its waters.
A low-born son who is a royal minister, a foolish son who is wise,
and the great wealth of a poor man— do not underestimate these among men.
The disciple who, out of greed for craft, learns that craft extensively,
would not even dare to speak of it, like one who sees a dream while mute.
A potter does not strive to beautify a jar lest it should break.
It is not for the sake of hurling students into the states of misery that one acts for their growth.
A man who serves the words of one who is poor,
weak, and lacking in wisdom is like a madman’s food.
By even a single tree that is in bloom and fragrant,
the entire grove is perfumed, just as a family is by a well-bred son.
A father who is a debtor is an enemy, as is a mother who is unchaste.
The wife is beautiful, yet the husband is a fool; the son is a fool, yet he is not unwise.
How can people distinguish between virtues and faults when they do not know the truth?
What concern has a blind man with perceiving the differences in forms?
The discernment of virtues and faults is achieved only through the teacher everywhere;
what greater rashness is there than to do so without the teacher?
A person who serves the base is degraded.
One who associates with equals never falls away;
by approaching the best, one quickly rises.
Therefore, one should associate with those who are superior to oneself.
One who clearly sees the present phenomenon here and there—
unshakable and unagitated— the wise person should cultivate that.
One who does not transgress the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion— [that person should be cultivated].
His fame increases like the moon in the bright fortnight:
the wise man who is endowed with virtue, gentle, eloquent,
humble in conduct, and free from arrogance— such a person gains renown.
Rare is a natural word of truth; rare is a son who brings security;
rare is a wife who is one's equal; rare is a dear kinsman.
Having attained great wealth, as well as knowledge and prosperity—
He who practices without being stubborn is called wise.
From the accumulation of what they have heard, the steadfast remain silent even when unasked,
yet they are full of well-spoken words, like a bell struck by a striker.
The wise man is like a drum when unasked, but becomes like rain when questioned;
the fool, however, whether asked or unasked, always prattles on excessively.
He is deaf to the censure of others and blind to the faults of others.
Like a lame man among other women, like a mindless cloth-dyer;
he was like a blind man though possessing eyes, like a deaf man though possessing ears;
like a mute man though possessing wisdom, like a weakling though possessing strength.
Then, when a crisis has arisen, one should lie down as if dead.
Having avoided evil friends, one should associate with the supreme person;
one should abide by his instruction, aspiring for unshakable happiness.
"It was too cold, it was too hot, it was too late"—
thus do purposes pass by for the youth who has neglected his duties.
But he who does not consider cold and heat as more than mere blades of grass;
One who performs the duties of a man does not fail to dwell in happiness.
In whatever place there is no respect, nor any who are dear or kinsmen,
nor any acquisition of knowledge, one should not dwell there for even a single day.
A wealthy man, one learned in the scriptures, a king, a river, and a thorn—these five are not found in whatever region they do not exist;
one should not dwell there for even a single day.
The moon is the ornament of the sky, and a husband is the ornament of women.
An ornament for the head is a king; knowledge is the ornament of all.
If one who seeks happiness seeks knowledge, let him abandon happiness;
for where is there knowledge for one who seeks happiness, and where is there happiness for one who seeks knowledge?
One should accomplish both knowledge and wealth moment by moment. Where is there knowledge for one who gives up at every moment? Where is there wealth for one who gives up at every moment?
The teacher takes a quarter, and the student, with understanding, takes a quarter.
One quarter [of victory] comes from fellow practitioners of the holy life, and one quarter through the passage of time.
Righteousness conquers, not unrighteousness; truth conquers, not falsehood;
patience conquers, not anger; the god conquers, not the coward.
Generosity is the ornament of the hand, truth the ornament of the throat, and learning the ornament of the ear; what need is there for other ornaments?
In foreign lands, wealth is knowledge; in times of misfortune, wisdom is wealth.
In the next world, Dhamma is wealth; indeed, virtue is wealth everywhere.
The moon is the lamp in the evening; the sun is the lamp at dawn;
Dhamma is the lamp for the three worlds; a good son is the lamp of the family.
Only the wise person truly understands the toil of the wise;
for a barren woman does not understand the heavy pain of childbirth.
For one who possesses no wisdom of their own, what can the Teacher do?
What will a mirror do for one who is deprived of eyes?
What will those who speak do where there is no ear?
What will a washerman do in a region of naked beggars?
Even a wise person comes to grief through association with wicked enemies, under the pretext of a deluded ascetic, and by supporting an unchaste woman.
There is no love equal to self-love; there is no wealth equal to grain.
There is no radiance equal to wisdom, and rain is indeed supreme among waters.
One should behave properly toward a serpent, a fire,
a renowned kshatriya, and a bhikkhu endowed with virtue.
Therefore, indeed, a wise person, clearly perceiving his own welfare,
should firmly establish faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
One who has reached the highest state of virtue does not dwell on a high bed.
Can a crow dwelling on the peak of a palace become a Garuḷa?
Seeing a danger yet to come, one should avoid it from afar;
seeing a danger that has arrived, the wise person remains unafraid.
Laziness is the stain of asceticism, neglect is the stain of a home;
sloth is the stain of beauty, and negligence is the stain of one who guards [virtue].
By degrees, the wise person, little by little, moment by moment, [should remove these stains].
As a smith removes the dross from silver, so should one cleanse oneself of impurities.
One should speak only what one would do, and not speak of that which one would not do;
for the wise clearly discern the man who speaks without acting.
Uneven ground, a place of danger, a strong wind, a concealed spot inhabited by deities,
a path, a battlefield, and a ford— these eight one should avoid.
One who is angry at night, one who is deluded, one who is conceited, one who is greedy, and likewise one who is lazy;
The one who dwells on single thoughts and the fool—these are destroyers of wealth.
The lustful, the hateful, and the deluded; the cowardly, the one heavy with worldly gain;
the woman, the drunkard, and the eunuch; and the child as the ninth.
There are ninety types of persons in the world—short-lived, wavering, and fickle;
what is kept secret when deliberated upon by these quickly becomes public knowledge.
One who does not study etymology, even if they study the Three Pitakas...
At every step he would falter, like a blind elephant in a forest.
But for him upon whose tongue-tip rests the lion of grammar— the Sutta, the Dhātu, the Gaṇa,
the Ōṇādika, and the Nāmaliṅgānusāsana— there is no stumbling.
One who is skilled in the characteristics of word-meanings and who has ascertained each specific characteristic is able,
without difficulty, to understand each respective part within the Three Piṭakas.
One who is proficient in the science of grammar is proficient in the Nighaṇḍu.
Constant application to the ornaments of prosody—
even one who is deficient in poetic composition—
indeed attains a place among poets and acquires a fame that is not insignificant.
Even when dried up, the sandalwood tree does not abandon its fragrance;
even when entering the mouth of a man, the elephant does not abandon its grace;
even when processed by a machine, the sugarcane does not abandon its sweet juice.
Even through suffering, the wise person does not abandon the Dhamma.
In dealings with wealth and grain, as well as in the acquisition of knowledge and learning,
in matters of food and worldly transactions, one should always be free from shame.
Natural eloquence, extensive and pure learning,
and tireless application— these are the causes for bondage here.
One should abandon evil friends and associate with wise people.
One should serve the virtuous and listen to the supreme Dhamma.
The doer of good reaps what is good, and the doer of evil reaps what is evil;
whatever kind of seed is sown, that is the kind of fruit one reaps.
Metre is the source of verses, and syllables are their manifestation;
verses are dependent on names, and the poet is the repository of verses.
Therefore, a wise person, clearly seeing his own welfare, [should study them].
One should honor the wise with reverence, as if they were a shrine.
One should see the steadfast, hear the steadfast, and dwell together with the steadfast.
One should engage in conversation and discourse with the steadfast, and take delight in them.
The wise person follows the right method and does not employ what is improper;
the right method is superior, and one who speaks correctly does not become angry.
Such a person understands discipline; it is good to associate with them.
If one should find a wise companion,
a steadfast one who dwells in virtue, walking together with him,
having overcome all dangers—
One should practice with a mind full of joy and mindfulness.
But if one does not find a wise companion to walk with—
one who is steadfast and lives a noble life— then one should rather dwell alone.
Like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom,
one should wander alone like an elephant in the Matanga forest.
There are thousands of occasions for sorrow and hundreds of occasions for fear.
Day after day fools fall into delusion, but not the wise.
Just as a jar is filled over a long time by the falling of drops of water,
so too are all branches of knowledge, the Dhamma, and wealth.
The wise, having encountered suffering, do not become despondent.
Having entered the mouth of Rāhu, what did the moon give back again?
They know a horse by its speed, and an ox by its yoke.
One knows a cow by its milk; one knows a wise man by his speech.
One should not reveal with words an action conceived in the mind, for success does not arise for one who performs deeds that are betrayed by others.
Poison is knowledge that has not been practiced; poison is food that has not been digested;
poison is an assembly for the poor; poison is a young wife for an old man.
Having eaten four or five morsels, one should drink water.
This is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute:
that man, though merely a commoner, is honored because he possesses virtuous qualities.
For what can a bow do, even if its bamboo is perfectly pure, if it lacks the necessary string?
The ascetic who is dissatisfied, the irascible one, the one who is constantly suspicious,
and the one who lives off the fortune of others— these six partake of suffering.
They are great beings, highly learned, yet they carry [the weight of their own faults].
Those deluded by greed fall into misfortune and become the source of four doubts:
regarding a well dug on a riverbank, a fire-drill, or a winnowing fan,
they do not say "there is no water" or similar words, yet such words issue from their own mouths.
One hears everything with the ear, and one sees everything with the eye;
yet the wise person does not deserve to heap up everything seen or heard.
Even from a fool, one should accept what is fitting and excellent, like pure gold.
What indeed does a lamp not illuminate within a delightful place?
Therefore, a wise person, clearly seeing their own self, should investigate the Dhamma with systematic reflection; in this way, one is purified therein.
Of what use is he who has been born, who robs his mother of her youth,
yet cannot even stand upright on the tip of his own bamboo pole like a banner?
Having examined thoroughly both the syllables and the positions, [one should know:]
The pupil may be a thief, while the teacher is a perpetrator of thievery.
The weapon that tames the untamed brings intoxication to the wicked;
it is like the light that creates vision for others but causes blindness to owls.
Long life is rare in this world, and true knowledge therein is very rare;
poetic composition is rare therein, and skill therein is very rare.
For, as a rule, when the destruction of beings is imminent, [these things are difficult to find].
Wrong paths stand in the guise of right paths, having gained access to the intellect.
A noble person is one endowed with such qualities as faith and virtue; he is the most excellent of human beings. (Sujanakaṇḍa)
Thus it was said by the Buddhas and others:

"A good and noble person is one who possesses these seven treasures: the treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of moral shame, the treasure of moral dread, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and wisdom is indeed the seventh treasure."
Whosoever, whether woman or man, possesses these riches, of them it is said, "They are not poor"; their life is not in vain.
Therefore, [one should cultivate] faith, virtue, serenity, and the vision of the Dhamma.
The wise person should apply themselves, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.
One should associate only with the virtuous and cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
having understood the true Dharma of the noble ones, one becomes better and not worse.
Avoid the company of the wicked; associate with the virtuous;
perform meritorious deeds day and night; constantly reflect upon impermanence.
He who is grateful, mindful of benefits, and wise—
He is a virtuous friend and possesses firm devotion;
he respectfully performs what needs to be done for one who is suffering—
such a person they call a true man.
A person who supports their mother and father, who honors those senior in their family,
who speaks gently and kindly, who has abandoned slanderous speech,
who is devoted to the removal of stinginess, who is truthful, and who has overcome anger— such a person [is truly noble].
The gods of the Thirty-three indeed call such a person a "true man.
Born of noble lineage, a son of good family, well-guarded in his ancestral line,
even when he has fallen into suffering himself, he would not perform a base deed.
The sun might rise in the west, Mount Meru might even bend,
the fire of men might become cool, and a blue lotus might bloom on a mountain peak—
but never would the speech of the virtuous ever change.
The shade of a tree is pleasant first to one's kinsmen and parents, then to one's teacher and the king, and manifoldly to the Buddha.
Bees desire flowers; the virtuous desire good qualities.
Flies seek what is putrid; the wicked seek out faults.
One who is base toward his mother is ill-spoken; one who is base toward his father is ill-doing.
One who is base toward both mother and father is both ill-spoken and ill-doing.
The mother is best when she speaks well; the father is best when he acts well.
Both mother and father are best when they speak well and act well.
A dog, seeing another dog, shows its teeth in order to do harm.
Upon seeing a good person, the wicked man seeks to provoke and harm them.
One should never perform actions with impulsive haste;
a fool who acts with rashness later comes to regret it.
Having slain anger, one never grieves;
the seers praise the abandonment of hypocrisy.
One should forgive all harsh speech that is uttered.
The virtuous call this patience supreme.
Dwelling in a cramped place that is impure and fearsome is painful;
more so than that is dwelling with an enemy or one who is disliked, and even more so than that is dwelling with one who is ungrateful.
One should advise and instruct, and restrain one from what is unwholesome;
for such a person is dear to the virtuous, but is disliked by the wicked.
One should conquer the harsh with gentleness, like a superior man conquers with non-violence.
One may conquer even a lowly person through small gifts and through effort.
Poison is not called poison; it is said that wealth belonging to the Saṅgha is poison.
Poison kills only one, but the wealth of the Saṅgha kills everyone.
Even a small amount of wealth is a support for the virtuous, like water in a well;
but even much wealth is no support for the wicked, like water in the ocean.
One should not desire what is unattainable, nor should one worry about what is inconceivable.
One should contemplate only the Dhamma; one should not desire time to be wasted.
For even that which was not thought of comes to pass, while that which was thought of perishes;
for wealth, whether for a woman or a man, does not arise from mere thinking.
He is dear to the wicked, but he does not show affection for the virtuous;
he delights in the doctrine of the wicked—this is a cause of downfall.
Virtues act as messengers for the good, even when they dwell far away.
Having smelled the fragrance of the ketaka flower, the bees depart of their own accord.
Karma performed in a previous birth—that is what is called "karma.
Therefore, one should strive with diligence to act in accordance with the character of a true man.
Just as a potter fashions whatever he desires from a lump of clay,
so does the young man proceed with the karma fashioned by himself.
Rising again and again, one should awaken to the great danger that has presented itself.
Of death, sickness, and sorrow, which one will fall upon me today?
As living beings stand in fear of themselves, so do they stand in fear of other beings;
by means of this analogy with oneself, the virtuous practice compassion toward all beings.
All tremble at the rod; all fear death.
Making oneself the analogy, one should neither kill nor cause to kill.
Whether he be a child, an elder, or a youth who has come to the house—
One should offer him worship, for a guest is venerable in every way.
Though surrounded by the wicked, he is auspicious when unassociated with them,
like a tall tree here that stands out from a dense thicket of undergrowth.
Endowed with bodily misconduct and other such evils,
this son of evil was proclaimed as "the fool" by the Lord of the World, the Master of Dhamma.
One who thinks what should not be thought, one who speaks what is ill-spoken,
one who performs misdeeds, and the wicked son of a fool— such a person, though very dear,
should not be treated as such, for he is a rogue who causes only trouble.
Even when carried on the head, it is like a pot half-filled with water.
A wicked snake and a wicked person—of these two, the wicked person is more wicked than the snake.
That snake can be pacified by mantras and medicinal herbs, but by what means is a wicked person pacified?
The fool who considers himself a fool is wise for that reason;
but the fool who fancies himself wise is called a fool indeed.
A fool considers [evil] as honey, so long as the evil has not yet ripened.
And when the evil ripens, then one encounters suffering.
It is not good for a powerful fool to acquire wealth through violence;
upon the breakup of the body, that person of poor wisdom is reborn in hell.
A wicked mouse at home, a wicked monkey in the forest, a wicked crow among birds, and a wicked brahmin among men.
Long is the night for one who stays awake; long is the league for one who is weary.
Long is the saṃsāra of fools who do not understand the true Dhamma.
One who is of a base nature does not see even a sesame seed’s worth of fault in others, nor even a slight malice;
yet he does not fail to see even a coconut’s worth of malice in himself.
One should know the fault of another, and one should know the fault of oneself;
like a tortoise hiding its limbs, one should observe the faults of others.
One should win over the greedy with wealth, and the stubborn with salutations.
The fool is deluded by compliance with his desires, while the wise man acts according to reality.
Just as the fruits of the Udumbara tree are red on the outside but filled within with maggots, so too is the heart of the wicked.
Even if a fool attends upon a wise man for as long as he lives,
he does not understand the Dhamma, just as a ladle does not know the taste of the soup.
If, while wandering, one should not find anyone better or even equal to oneself...
One should make a firm resolve for the solitary life; there is no companionship with fools.
For those who are unarisen, undecayed, and unconfused, the first [state] is better than the last;
for the latter causes suffering but once, while the former does so at every step.
One should not engage in enmity with a wicked person, nor should one form friendship with them;
hot embers burn, while cold ones only blacken the hand.
That a wicked person speaks kindly is no reason for trust.
Honey stays upon the tip of the tongue, while the halāhala poison is in the heart.
A wicked person should be avoided, even if adorned with knowledge;
for is a snake not terrifying, even when decorated with a jewel?
For the virtuous appear like coconuts even when seen from the outside;
others are like jujube fruits, charming only on the surface.
Furthermore, they are like [a fruit] that is ripe within but has thorns on the outside.
The hearts of the virtuous are thus filled with nectar within,
just as the ripe udumbara fruit is red only on the outside;
the hearts of the wicked are thus filled with poison within, just as the kimila fruit is red throughout.
One who refrains from action out of fear of blame—what manhood is that?
For who, indeed, does not diminish their food out of fear of old age?
Drinking milk for serpents only serves to increase their venom.
For instruction is not for the remedy of anger in those who are deluded.
One should neither stand nor walk anywhere in the company of a wicked person;
for a wicked person gives only suffering, never any happiness.
Those who are unbound are bound in that place where fools shine forth;
those who are bound are released in that place where the wise shine forth.
Just as one who has climbed onto a small piece of wood might sink in the great ocean, so it is with the fool.
Thus, by relying on the lazy, even one who lives rightly sinks down;
therefore, one should avoid that lazy person of inferior energy.
One who is endowed with faith, virtue, and the like, possessing good friends and noble companions—
One who desires progress and possesses discernment should cultivate such a friend.
Indeed, a friend should be gladdened by the highest virtues, such as generosity;
a wise person should associate with such a one with a mind free from guile.
One who acts for one's welfare is a true kinsman, while even a kinsman who acts for one's harm is no kinsman at all.
Disease born of the body is harmful, whereas the medicinal herbs of the forest are beneficial.
One who destroys what must be done in one's absence, yet speaks sweet words when face-to-face, is a mere flatterer.
One should avoid such a friend as one would a jar of poison with milk on its surface.
When wealth is lost, even friends, wives, children, and siblings abandon one;
yet when wealth is present, they all serve the wealthy man, for in this world, wealth is the great companion.
One should recognize a servant by his sending of messages, a kinsman by the arrival of misfortune,
a friend in times of calamity, and a wife when wealth is exhausted. Likewise, one recognizes them in festivals,
in times of distress, in famine, and in conflict with enemies.
He who stands at the king’s gate or in the charnel ground is a kinsman.
One should not trust an enemy, nor should one trust even a friend;
for when a friend is provoked to anger, he reveals every fault.
A mother, a friend, and a father—these are naturally beneficial to one.
Others become well-wishers through the performance of service.
One should know a friend in times of misfortune, a hero in battle, and a pure person in debt.
He who wishes to reconcile again with a wife whose wealth has been exhausted,
with a kinsman in times of misfortune, or with a friend who has once proved treacherous—
he embraces death, just as a she-mule conceives a foal.
A remainder of debt, a remainder of fire, and likewise a remainder of disease—these increase again and again; therefore, one should not leave a remainder.
He whose face is like a lotus and whose speech is as cool as sandalwood—
One should not attend upon such a person who has *halāhala* poison in their heart.
One should not serve a harsh master, nor should one serve a miserly one;
therefore, avoid such a master, for he is not to be restrained.
One should avoid from afar a bad country, a bad friend, a bad family, bad kinsmen, a bad wife, and a bad slave.
One who is cool in speech has many friends; one who is harsh has few friends.
An analogy should be understood here from the kings of the sun and the moon:
the prevention of harm, the application toward what is beneficial,
and not abandoning one in times of misfortune— this is the characteristic of a friend.
One who is dear, respected, and inspiring; who speaks appropriately and is patient with one's words;
who delivers profound discourse and does not urge one toward what is improper—a wise person desiring prosperity should cultivate such a friend.
One who is dear, respected, and disciplined, who speaks appropriately and is patient with words,
who delivers profound discourse and does not urge one toward what is improper—
in such a person these qualities are found here.
Therefore, one who desires a friend, out of compassion and seeking his welfare,
should associate with such a person— even if he is being led away.
This applies to one’s own offspring, those with whom a bond has been formed, and likewise those descended through one’s lineage.
A friend who guards one from calamities—thus should a friend be known to be fourfold:
one who is dear, one who is respected, one who is worthy of esteem, and one who speaks what is beneficial while being patient with one's words;
one who offers profound counsel and does not urge one toward what is improper.
One who desires friends should serve such a friend for as long as life lasts—one who is dear, respected, and worthy of esteem; who speaks and is patient with what is said;
who offers profound counsel and does not urge one toward what is improper.
One who desires prosperity and possesses discernment should cultivate such a friend.
[This concludes] the Chapter on Kings: he who pleases the populace by means of all four bases of popularity.
"One who rules is called a king in the world"— thus should the wise man observe.
Generosity, beneficial conduct, kind speech, and impartiality—
these four means of integration were proclaimed by the Lord of Sages.
Generosity, beneficial conduct, kind speech, and impartiality—
by performing these four means of attracting many through the quality of not disparaging others, one goes to heaven.
Generosity, pleasant speech, and beneficial conduct here in this world...
And impartiality toward all things, as is appropriate in each case—
these indeed are the means of integration in the world, like the linchpin of a moving chariot:
generosity, virtue, renunciation, uprightness, gentleness, and austerity.
Absence of anger, non-violence, patience, and non-opposition—
these ten qualities a king should maintain with diligence.
A king should sleep for one watch, and a wise man likewise for two watches.
A householder has three watches of the night, but a beggar has four.
A house is empty without a son; a kingdom is empty without a king;
the mouth of one without a craft is empty; but poverty is the emptiness of all things.
One who desires wealth should engage in trade; one who desires knowledge should associate with the learned;
one who desires a son should seek a young woman; and a king should appoint a minister when the need arises.
For birds, the sky is their strength; for fish, water is their strength.
The strength of the weak is the king; the strength of princes is weeping.
Forgiveness, wakefulness, rising [from sleep], sharing, and compassion—these are the virtues of a leader that the virtuous should always desire.
Kings speak but once; recluses and brahmins speak but once;
so do the true persons in the world; this is the eternal law.
A lazy householder who indulges in sensual pleasures is not good.
One who has gone forth without self-restraint is not good;
a king who acts without reflection is not good;
and a wise man who is prone to anger is not good.
One should know for oneself the arrival of one's own destruction; one should know for oneself what has been done and what remains to be done;
one should know who deserves restraint and who deserves encouragement.
A mother [knows] the evil committed by her son, and likewise a teacher [knows] that committed by his pupil.
The king [overcomes] the evil done by the realm, the chaplain [overcomes] that done by the king.
One should conquer anger with non-anger, overcome the wicked with goodness;
one should conquer the miser with generosity, and the speaker of falsehood with truth.
The gift that tames the untamed is a gift that accomplishes all aims.
Through giving and through pleasant speech, people rise up and bow down.
The gift that tames the untamed is a gift; the absence of giving is what corrupts the tamed.
By means of giving and pleasant speech, people rise up and fall down.
Giving is the medicine for affection; stinginess is the medicine for hatred.
Giving is the medicine for fame; stinginess is the medicine for wretchedness.
One should never enjoy sensual pleasures equal to those of a king—
neither his deportment, nor his choice of foods, nor his garlands, perfumes, and ointments,
nor any clothing or ornaments; one should not act like a king.
"The king is not my friend, nor is the king my equal;
'He is my master,' thus one should establish certainty in the mind.
One should dwell neither too far from the king, nor too close, but in a breezy place."
One should not go too near nor too far, nor should one sit on a high seat in the presence of the master;
a servant should avoid these six faults and remain as self-restrained as fire.
One should not stand behind, nor in front, nor too close, nor too far away.
Neither in a marshy place, nor in a headwind, nor where the wind blows from both sides;
having avoided these faults, they stood to one side with prayers,
incantations, and well-spoken words.
Whether by means of a gift or through tradition,
in whatever way and wherever one may find benefit,
in that very way and in that very place should one exert effort.
Whether it be a farmer, a merchant, a commoner, an ascetic, or one of noble birth—
if these are prosperous, the kingdom will also be prosperous;
if they are weak, the kingdom will also be weak.
Therefore, one who bears the burden of the kingdom should protect the vast realm.
He who plucks the unripe fruit from a great,
fruit-bearing tree does not know its flavor, and its seed is destroyed.
A kingdom that rules by unrighteousness is like a great tree;
it does not know its own essence, and the kingdom perishes.
It is like one who plucks a ripe fruit from a great, fruit-bearing tree.
He discerns its flavor, and its seed does not perish.
The kingdom which one rules righteously is like a great tree:
he discerns its flavor, and the kingdom does not perish.
Those without a leader perish; those with many leaders perish;
those led by women perish; and those led by children perish.
Just as when cattle are crossing a ford, if the lead bull goes straight,
all the cows go straight because their leader has gone straight.
Even so among humans, he who is esteemed as the best—
Thus, if he practices the Dhamma, how much more so will the rest of the people.
Just as when bulls are crossing a ford, if the lead bull goes straight,
all the cows go straight, because the leader has gone straight.
In the same way, among human beings, whoever is considered the best—
if he practices the Dhamma, let alone the rest of the people—
the entire kingdom dwells in happiness, provided the king is righteous.
He said that there is no destruction through having many leaders;
rather, lotuses withered and perished because of the seven [types of] enemies.
There should be diligent protection by means of well-guarded watchfulness, and the protection of the family through proper conduct.
For true knowledge is what prevents a clansman who is a leader from being negligent.
Regarding the section on sons:
the wise desire a son who is well-born and born after [the father] in accordance with his lineage.
They do not desire one who is base-born, who brings disgrace upon the family.
Seeing five grounds, the wise desire a son:
"He will support us when we are supported by him, or he will perform our duties."
The family lineage shall endure for long, and he will receive his inheritance;
or else, he will provide an offering for the deceased.
A father who has many sons must always support them alone.
Even those with many sons cannot support their father alone.
One may ill-treat a son or a brother, yet one should not abandon them;
for what harm is there in cutting off a foot that is smeared with impurity?
The section on the physician’s training:
One who has practiced the science of longevity, who is pleasing to behold by all,
and who is endowed with the virtues of noble conduct— such a person is designated as a physician.
The knowledge of various texts, the thorough vision of the perfection of kamma,
dexterity, swiftness of hand, clarity, heroic power,
naturalness, momentary knowledge, and well-spoken words.
Zeal, being competent in all respects, and the practice of medicine are the characteristics [of a physician]. Soiled clothing, anger, arrogance,
and going uninvited— these five should be avoided.
Seeing the task, compassion, skill, and knowledge of the tradition—
these four virtues of a good physician are recognized by the wise.
The signs of victory over disease, the taste, and the medicine [are likewise required].
The distinction between the three characteristics must indeed be understood by the physician.
[Regarding slaves:
one born in the house, one bought with wealth, and one who has entered into slavery of his own accord.
Thus, there are four kinds of servants: one who rises before [the master],
one who lies down after, one who takes only what is given,
and one who performs good deeds and carries away fame and praise.

Dāsā 0.0177: The five types of persons who are like friends, kinsmen, and one’s own self—namely, thieves, those who are wise, and likewise those who are to be understood by the wise, as well as a friend’s wife and relatives.
(The Chapter on Women)
Women of the world are called "hopes"; no limit exists for them.
They are impassioned and insolent, like a fire that consumes everything.
Therefore, having abandoned them, the wise man should cultivate seclusion.
Women of the world are indeed desires; no limit exists for them.
Full of passion and impudent, they are like a fire that consumes everything.
Abandoning them, I shall go forth into homelessness, cultivating seclusion.
In this world, one should avoid from afar those known as women who are prone to anger,
who cause dissension among friends, who are backbiters, and who are ungrateful—
just as one avoids a river, a road, a tavern, an assembly hall, and a brothel.
Thus, the wise do not become angry with women of the world.
All rivers have winding courses; all forests are made of wood;
and all women commit evil when they find a secluded place.
A woman is like a water-pot, and a man there is like glowing embers;
therefore, a wise person should not place the pot and the fire in one spot.
To women, wealth and beauty are their riches; for men, knowledge is their wealth.
Virtue is the wealth of monks, and strength is the wealth of kings.
A woman is well-pleased with five things, archers with seven things,
a good wife with one month [of provisions], and students with half a month [of provisions].
One should praise another when they are old; a wife when her youth has passed;
a hero when he has returned from battle; and grain when it has come home.
A woman with two husbands, and a monk with two dwellings.
Between a bird and one with two feet, which is more numerous?
Without the night there is no moon; without waves there is no ocean;
without swans there is no lotus pond; and without a husband, a woman has no beauty.
The ascetic who is discontented is lost, as is the one who, though content, makes further aspirations;
the modest courtesan is lost, as are the shameless women of good family.
Among these women of many wiles, who are thieves, truth is exceedingly difficult to find.
The state of sloth is difficult to perceive, like a fish that has gone into the water.
Those who speak softly are like fires; they are as hard to satisfy as rivers.
Recognizing them for what they are, one should sink away from them and avoid them from afar.
The great illusion that ensnares, which disturbs the holy life—knowing it, they sink; one should avoid it from afar.
For even some women, O lord of men, are better than a man.
Wise, virtuous, devoted to her mother-in-law and faithful to her husband—
the man born of such a woman shall be a hero, a lord of the earth.
The son of such a fortunate woman may even rule a kingdom. One may converse with one who holds a sword in hand,
or even converse with a malevolent spirit (pisāca).
One might even step upon a venomous snake, bitten by which one does not live;
but one should never converse alone with a woman.
For it is not the case that a man is wise in all circumstances.
A woman too can be wise, discerning in every circumstance.
For it is not the case that a man alone is wise in all situations;
a woman too can be wise, swiftly contemplating what is beneficial.
Well water, the shade of a banyan tree, and a house of bricks—
these are cool in the heat and warm in the cold.
As for women, some are indeed said by the Sage to be like a bed.
She is the best of women among attendants, the foremost of those who serve.
(From the *Pakiṇṇakakaṇḍa*):
Endowed with noble birth, virtue, and qualities, he is devoted to all that is wholesome.
Skilled in lute-playing, observant of the sending of messengers, and observant of the Dhamma;
one who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, devoted to recitation and burnt offerings,
and intent on words of benediction— such a person is the royal chaplain.
Kappa, Vyākaraṇa, Joti, Sattha, Sikkhā, and Nirutti, along with Chandoviciti—
these they call the six Vedangas. One who grasps the meaning from what is said once,
who is light-handed [in composition], and has mastered the phonemes;
One who surveys all the sciences, known as an eminent scribe,
learned in the treatises on the complete rules of policy, equal to a horse fully laden in carrying burdens,
and endowed with the qualities of a brave hero— such a person is appointed as the commander-in-chief of the army.
One who is wise, eloquent in speech, intelligent, capable of discerning the minds of others, steadfast, and a speaker of things as they truly are—
such a person is prescribed as an envoy. One endowed with the virtues of a son and grandson,
learned in the scriptures, and a connoisseur of flavors [is also suitable].
One who is brave and firm is called a cook.
One who understands gestures, facial expressions, and the truth, who is strong,
pleasant to look upon, diligent, and always skillful, is called an attendant.
Where is virtue for one mixed with women? Where is compassion for one who eats meat?
Where is truthfulness for one who drinks liquor? Where is modesty in great greed?
Where is craft for one who is greatly indolent? Where is wealth for one who is greatly wrathful?
The liquor-addict, the time-server, the one who attends social gatherings,
the frivolous, the rogue, the evil friend, the lazy, and the squanderer of wealth—
these five, though living, are described by Vyāsa as being dead.
The suffering one, the sick, the deluded, the debtor, the servant,
the sleepy, the negligent, the happy one, the fool afflicted by disease, the lustful,
and the one who delights in work— these seven are excluded from the Teacher’s [teaching].
Because they support all householders and are the givers of wealth,
one should therefore honor and revere one’s parents just as one would any other kinsman—
be it mother, father, brother, or others.
Cows are our supreme friends, from whom medicinal herbs are born.
They are givers of food, givers of strength, givers of beauty, and likewise givers of happiness.
Knowing this truth, they did not kill those cows.
Those who eat beef eat as if they were eating their own mother's flesh;
when those [cows] have died, vultures will feast upon them and carry them away in their beaks.
The nourishment for women is twofold, and their intelligence is fourfold.
Exertion has five qualities, while sensual desire has eight.
A fool who praises only asceticism does not shine in the world;
yet one who possesses true knowledge shines even in a covered well.
Seeing laziness as fear and the arousal of energy as safety,
be those who have aroused energy— this is the instruction of the Buddha.
Seeing dispute as fear and non-dispute as safety...
Be united and harmonious; this is the instruction of the Buddhas.
Seeing heedlessness as fear and heedfulness as security, develop the Eightfold Path; this is the instruction of the Buddhas.
Censure and praise are impermanent and temporary;
they are trivial and merely partial. A wise person should not look to them, but rather look to what is righteous and unrighteous, what is beneficial and harmful, and what is good and evil.
In the western region, within a distance of four gāvutas from the city of Kāverīpattana, there was a beautiful village known as Kanaraya,
where the merchant Pakhukkūpuraseṭṭhi was renowned during his later years.
Together with the two [masters] Dviveda and Sākamhi, who were born in that same place, he—
who had previously mastered the *Suttas* in Laṅkā, Bhārata, and other lands,
and who was well-trained in the *Tipiṭaka* by the renowned Ārāma-sīha— [composed this].
In the presence of those who performed the task of the Council for nine years,
and also in the presence of those dwelling at Dakkhiṇārāma who were well-versed and wise;
having trained for twenty-seven years, the illustrious one [attained mastery].
While residing in the excellent city of Sundara, which was beautiful, renowned, and auspicious,
and while dwelling with Jotipāla in Sundara, he who recites the Gaṇa [scriptures],
relying upon the Peṭaka and many books of various systems (nīti).
Even though this best of books has been made subject to decay,
may this book of mine remain as long as the Teaching lasts—
remaining indeed for those who are well-disciplined, possessing excellent essence, and clearly elucidated.
By this most distinguished merit and by other deeds,
may I go to the auspicious deathless state, just as Maṇisībhigu did.
“The trees are now like glowing coals, O Blessed One.”
“Just as the month of Rammaka, O Brahmin, among the summer months,
shines forth even more than other months because of its flowering trees;
so too does the forest thicket shine when its tops are in full bloom.”
"In the first month of summer, in the heat of the season"—
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One;
this is the declaration of homage.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem and to my teacher, the preeminent among poets,
I shall compose the *Tammāsavasika* meter, which consists of twelve months.
Indeed, the month of *Cittasammata* shines forth even more than others.
The month of Rammaka is a delightful month; by that very name it shall be known.
In that month of Sucitta, the nāga trees are in full bloom;
the asana trees are flowering, and they truly waft their fragrance throughout the forest.
A great festival was celebrated during that month;
splashing one another with scented water, they rejoiced greatly.
Just as the month of Rammaka occurs among the summer months, O Brahmin;
It does not shine with other flowers as it does with the *dumapuppha*.
On the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight of the month of Citta, at dawn,
the Fully Enlightened One took up his excellent bowl and robe.
Out of compassion for the nāgas, he came to Nāgadīpa.
Indeed, the month called Vesākha was most distinguished and well-known,
being specially marked by the peaceful ones in honor of the Lord of the World.
During that month of Vesākha, even the campaka trees blossomed beautifully;
noble people rejoiced after sprinkling water upon the Bodhi tree.
Like young fawns in the forests, they leaped about in every direction.
Chanting in the assembly, the nectar for the ears of the people,
on the second day at the time of the meal being announced, the Victor, the Lord of Sages,
was in the delightful month of Vesākha, on the full moon day.
The month esteemed as the eldest (Jeṭṭha) is also renowned among the followers of the Sugata as possessing auspicious marks,
for it is indeed endowed with the "eldest" (jeṭṭha). In that month of Jeṭṭha,
there are the jasmine (sumana), the forest jasmine (vanamallikā), and so forth.
They blossomed and blew forth, enchanting all people.
Even the noble partridges (*khañjarīṭa*) became present within the circle of the forest;
for indeed, at that time, the eldest star, Kṛttikā, blazed forth in that very place.
The month named Āsāḷha was also exceedingly distinguished;
for it was in that month that the wise Sage, the Buddha, took rebirth,
as well as his Great Renunciation and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
They perform the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) right there as well. There,
the *puṇṇāga* trees are in bloom, scattering their fragrance in every direction,
and the sun stands at that very place, at the northernmost tip of its course.
In the month of Sāvaṇa, during the time of Siha,
virtuous humans, having faith in the Three Jewels, offer the supreme gift of the tally-sticks (salākā).
Even the Kaṭeruha flowers bloom in that month of Sāvaṇa.
Indeed, even the constellation of Savana shone with extraordinary brilliance. And within a year,
the monks who were the heart-sons of the Sugata, dwelling in comfort,
undertook the work of receiving the recitation [of the scriptures].
At that time, the people of Manu’s lineage held great festivals on boats that were esteemed as being like young maidens,
filled with water in rivers, and resembling mats of woven grass.
They even celebrated grand processions by boat.
Men and women play and rejoice in the conquered realm;
even the golden *yamadū* trees then truly blossom,
while the cloud rains down and lets fall snow in gentle showers.
In the month of Vassika, during the month of Assayuja,
lotuses and other water-born flowers bloom in many ways, truly delightful to the mind.
With rows of great lamps, the entire surface of the earth became radiant.
The virtuous people of the Sugata’s fold worship the Lord of the World.
Having completed the rains retreat, those whose wealth is their austerity wander in every direction;
like those who are liberal in giving, these virtuous ones feel as if they are being cooled by a refreshing breeze.
Even during the most excellent month of Kattika, human beings rejoice;
the *kosītakī* flowers bloom and the winds blow.
Furthermore, virtuous people bestow the great gift of the Kathina robe.
At that time, even the rays of the moon were exceedingly bright.
There was a fall of snow, and a northern wind blew;
for indeed, the festival of the Kattika full moon was taking place then.
In the month of Āsāḷha, known as Dhanu-rāsī, during the season esteemed as winter;
when the one worthy of supreme worship, the Wielder of the Spear, was honored, the assembly hall was also put into operation.
Flowers esteemed by the gods, lovely and delightful, [were offered].
In that month, the flowers bloom and there is a fall of snow;
the rice fields ripen upon the earth,
and the constellation Mṛgaśiras shines in the expanse of the sky.
In the month of Phussa, during the syllable *Makāra*, the blossoms of the sunīla creeper—
so enchanting to people— bloom and waft their fragrance. Even kings,
having crushed their enemies’ bones, arrange them into military formations.
The assembly, including the elephants, horses, and others, gazed on him. On that day—
the eighth and full moon— at the solstice of the sun’s southern course,
the sun was honored by the world even though it was exceedingly cool.
In the ninth month after his enlightenment,
on the full moon day of Phussa, the Victor arrived at Laṅkādīpa to purify it.
In the months of Kumbha and Māgha, the cotton trees were in full bloom.
They bestow sweet nectar upon human beings.
Even the great festival of sacrifice became manifest on the surface of the earth;
and in all other places, even the clouds thundered and rained down.
Men and women are charming, with beautiful feet and lovely garments;
even the *pucimanda* trees bear fresh leaves.
In this month of Phagguṇa, it is fragrant and beautiful.
The trees in the forest are in bloom and shine with new leaves.
Indeed, a breeze blows from the southern region there;
having fashioned sand stupas upon the sandy ground, they would pay them homage.
In the first month of summer, various trees burst into bloom;
by this, the entire forest was indeed variegated and beautiful to behold.
While Jotipāla was renowned, he was famous in his own home.
This was composed by the scribe while residing at Neka-gantha.
